items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: When Dizzy was sick we took this picture, we love you Dizzy, to send to him.

ctx.x: Oh yeah, as I was digging out, I don’t know I was going through looking for other things and I happened to find, I’ve got a whole archive in my house man, because I’m one of those people who saved everything. I’ve got newspaper clippings from Count Basie when I was with his band in the 50s in Europe. In fact I’ve got some pay receipts from Lionel Hampton from 1948, just because I kept all these things. Anyway, these are the members of Count Basie’s band. These are alumni. Because I think in this picture there’s…

band leader friend. This was taken on a tour with Randy Weston, when Dizzy Gillespie was sick. We were in Europe at the time. This is Randy of course, this is Talib Kibwe, this is Stafford James and me, and Eric Assasnte, that’s his name, Eric Ajie is the comic. Eric Assante. When Dizzy was sick we took this picture, we love you Dizzy, to send to him. Again, this is taken at the same party and the same people. I don’t know who this gentleman is at the top here. Do you recognize him?

items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Dizzy Gillespie one time we were in Perugia, Italy and about two o’clock in the afternoon, we had come in to the town and we were going out to get some lunch or something.

ctx.x: Billy Eckstine put one under the pillow that Basie sat on. So when he sat down — oh, can you imagine that man? You know people would say, because, actually, musicians can become like little — we all have little boys left around in us. We all, Dizzy Gillespie

certainly was one. Boy I guess I’m going through a lot of stories. One brings on another one. Dizzy Gillespie one time we were in Perugia, Italy and about two o’clock in the afternoon, we had come in to the town and we were going out to get some lunch or something. There was a man in the lobby with a puppet on a string. And he was doing nice little things, making the puppet do a lot of stuff. Anyway, Dizzy Gillespie got interested in this thing, so this was about two or three o’clock in the afternoon. And I think…

Let me ask you a couple of questions about that. Do you think that in jazz education today that we’re missing something because there aren’t these funny little things that find their way into the music?
